To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sex differences in developmental plasticity and sex specific fitness effects of colour morphs have consequences for population structure, local adaptations and polymorphisms in pygmy grass-hoppers.

(1) colour polymorphisms are maintained in Tetrix grasshoppers by frequency-dependent selection, (2) sex differences in the expression of colour polymorphisms, and sex by environment interactions, are important for the maintenance of colour polymorphic variation, and (3) the maintenance of colour morphs is facilitated by sex differences in plasticity and developmental stability.

(1) sex differences are important for evolution in heterogeneous environments, (2) sex differences can be important for the evolution of local adaptations, (3) sex differences in development and plasticity can be important for evolution in changing and dynamic environments, and (4) sex differences are relevant for the maintenance of polymorphisms and for the evolution of sexual dimorphism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of adaptive variation and the evolution of polymorphisms in spatially heterogeneous, temporally changing and dynamic fitness landscapes.
the evolution of local adaptations in a heterogeneous and temporally variable environment, and how this is influenced by sex-specific selection and developmental plasticity.
how local adaptation and evolution of sex differences are affected by environmental variation in heterogeneous and changing environments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have learned much from studies of sex differences in local adaptation in pygmy grasshop- pers, and that we have also identified a number of questions that need further research.
sex differences are important for evolution, but we do not know exactly how and when.
the role of sex for evolution in heterogeneous, changing environments and dynamic landscapes is complex and context dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sex differences are important for evolution, but the mechanisms by which sex differences affect evolution are complex, and the outcomes are unpredictable.
we have shown that sex differences are important for evolution in heterogeneous environments, and that the evolution of sex-specific traits can be driven by selection on the other sex.

we found that (1) colour morphs differ in their developmental plasticity, (2) colour morphs are locally adapted, (3) colour morphs have different genetic architecture, and (4) sex differences in development and plasticity have consequences for population dynamics, local adaptations and the maintenance of polymorphisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sex differences in the relationships linking phenotypic traits with fitness, and sex specific developmental responses to environmental variation, can have important evolutionary consequences.
sex differences are an essential part of the evolution of adaptive variation.
sex differences in the expression of adaptive traits and in the responses to selection may be an important driver for the evolution of local adaptations, population differentiation and speciation.
